answer.rationale: The binding constraint is not cost alone but cost-under-fragility: the line is at 94% of committed volume with no buffer and the contract lapses in 14 days. That combination rules out any option requiring qualification or migration work inside the window, which is why memory_c2 (switching to the low-cost vendor) is the tempting but wrong read — its consolidated form records the upside (sharp unit-cost cut, quick onboarding, clean invoicing) with no record of what the buffer conditions were at the time, and a switch executed against a full line with 14 days of runway is a different action than the one that memory describes. I want the archived source for c2 specifically to see whether that onboarding happened with slack in the system; if it did, the memory does not transfer. Similarly, add_second_source (memory_c3) is the right structural move but the wrong cycle — qualification lead time exceeds 14 days, so it buys resilience only after the cliff it is meant to cover. defer_decision (memory_c5) is disqualified on its own terms: that memory is explicitly about a non-critical renewal that continued month-to-month, and this contract does not auto-renew, so deferring here means lapsing, not coasting. That leaves negotiate_terms, which is the only path that touches the 18% mandate without introducing new delivery risk, since it keeps the incumbent integration intact (memory_c1). I am verifying memory_c4 because my whole case rests on it: I need the original record to see what the benchmarking actually consisted of and how much price and payment-term movement was really obtained, since a consolidated 'recovered real margin' could be anywhere from 2% to 15% and only the upper end makes a dent in an 18% target. I am deliberately scoping this as a guarded move rather than reaching for memory_c6's multi-year volume commitment: locking a long term to hit this year's number would trade away the option to add a second source or requalify once the line has buffer, and c6's upside was recorded without any note of what flexibility it cost. So: negotiate a short bridge term with benchmarked pricing, and hold the structural fixes for the next review. Residual uncertainty I am not resolving: negotiation alone probably will not deliver the full 18%, and I should say so rather than let a partial win be reported as the mandate met. If c4's source shows the recovered margin was thin, the honest output is a shortfall flagged to finance plus a queued second-source qualification, not a rushed vendor switch against a line with no slack.
